imageAlt: Batik silk sari patterned with creepers and curling foliage

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik; wax resist and natural dyes

summary: This silk sari was made in Santiniketan in the 1930s–1940s and belongs to the collection of Umang Hutheesing.
description: Executed in batik using wax resist and natural dyes, the sari demonstrates the experimental approach to textile design that developed at Santiniketan through the adaptation of batik techniques associated with Java.

The design is centred on a controlled vocabulary of creepers, curling foliage and stylised vegetal forms. Rather than covering the surface with dense ornament, the foliage is carefully distributed across the field, allowing the ground to remain an active part of the composition. The restrained use of branching stems and curling leaves creates a sense of movement while maintaining a clear rhythm across the textile. The larger vegetal forms are articulated through the resist process, with wax defining the contours and preserving selected areas against successive applications of dye.

The sari is particularly evocative of Santiniketan's interest in translating nature into a disciplined visual language. The creeper is not treated as a botanical representation but as a flexible ornamental element—its stems bending, branching and curling to establish continuity across the surface. Through the controlled repetition and variation of these forms, the design occupies a space between drawing, painting and textile ornament. The use of natural dyes further contributes to the organic character of the composition, while the wax-resist technique gives the foliage a distinctive linear quality.

As a work of Santiniketan batik, the sari reflects an important moment when an Indonesian technique was reinterpreted through local artistic practices, transforming the language of vegetal ornament into a distinctly Santiniketan mode of textile expression.

imageAlt: Batik silk sari by Ketaki Roy Chowdhury, 1974

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik; wax resist and natural dyes in three colours

summary: This silk sari was made by Ketaki Roy Chowdhury at Kala Bhavana on 15 September 1974, during her period of study there, and was gifted to her elder sister on her wedding.
description: Executed in batik using wax resist and three natural colours, the sari reflects Roy Chowdhury’s close engagement with the visual environment of Santiniketan.

Its imagery draws from her encounters with clay maquettes and models of Bengal, folk-art forms seen at the Poush Mela, elephants and other figurative forms. These elements are arranged as a lively and personal vocabulary, recalling the objects, performances and popular visual culture she encountered in Santiniketan rather than relying on a fixed ornamental scheme.

The sari is particularly significant for Roy Chowdhury’s attempt to move beyond the established vocabulary of Santiniketan batik associated with Karu Sangha and Kala Bhavana. By this period, batik at Santiniketan had developed a recognisable design language, strongly informed by the vegetal rhythms, figures and compositional principles derived from Ajanta. Roy Chowdhury deliberately sought other sources, turning instead to the folk and material culture immediately around her.

Her approach demonstrates how students at Kala Bhavana could work within an established batik tradition while also questioning and extending its visual vocabulary. The sari brings together the technical discipline of wax-resist batik with forms rooted in Santiniketan’s lived cultural landscape, making it both a record of artistic education and a personal expression of the place and period in which it was made.

imageAlt: Batik silk sari by Ketaki Roy Chowdhury, 1976

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik; wax resist and acid colours

summary: This silk sari was made by Ketaki Roy Chowdhury at Kala Bhavana on 20 December 1976 as a gift for another sister’s wedding.
description: The design brings together elements of Javanese batik and the established vocabulary of Santiniketan batik, reflecting Roy Chowdhury’s continued engagement with different textile traditions.

The principal motifs are the tumpal and stylised flame forms, characteristic elements of Javanese batik. Two opposing tumpals are placed face to face and joined by a floral motif drawn from the Santiniketan design vocabulary. This arrangement creates a dialogue between the geometric structure of the Javanese forms and the flowing vegetal language associated with Santiniketan, while the symmetry gives the composition a strong rhythmic order.

The use of acid colours gives the sari a particularly vivid and intense chromatic character. Their highly saturated tones heighten the contrast between the tumpal, flame and floral forms, giving the composition a striking visual energy. The brightness of the palette also lends the traditional motifs a more contemporary and experimental quality.

Made for a familial occasion, the sari demonstrates Roy Chowdhury’s ability to combine Javanese design elements with Santiniketan’s batik vocabulary, while using colour and composition to move beyond established conventions. It is both a personal wedding gift and an example of her continuing experimentation with the possibilities of batik at Kala Bhavana.

imageAlt: Batik cotton coverlet by Ketaki Roy Chowdhury, 1972

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Cotton, batik; wax resist and dyes

summary: This batik coverlet was made by Ketaki Roy Chowdhury at Kala Bhavana in 1972 and was used as a backdrop at Amrakunja during Indira Gandhi’s visit to Santiniketan.
description: Conceived on a larger scale than a wearable textile, the work demonstrates the potential of batik as a medium for expansive figurative compositions.

The imagery is inspired by the relief sculptures of Mahabalipuram, with figures of Brahma, Ganesha and a Yakshinitranslated into the linear language of wax-resist batik. Rather than reproducing the sculptures literally, Roy Chowdhury interprets their sculptural volumes and distinctive silhouettes through simplified contours and patterned surfaces. The figures are given a strong presence across the textile, allowing the coverlet to function simultaneously as an ornamental backdrop and a large-scale pictorial work.

The choice of Mahabalipuram as a source reflects the wider engagement at Kala Bhavana with Indian sculptural and architectural traditions, while the translation of stone relief into batik demonstrates the medium’s capacity to move between painting, drawing and textile. Made for a significant public occasion at Amrakunja, the coverlet also illustrates how batik could extend beyond clothing and domestic use into the ceremonial and visual environment of Santiniketan.

imageAlt: Batik tussar silk shirt by Ketaki Roy Chowdhury, 1976

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Tussar silk, batik; wax resist and natural sogan dye

summary: This tussar silk shirt was made by Ketaki Roy Chowdhury in 1976 as a gift for her fiancé.
description: The surface is patterned throughout with a vocabulary of Javanese batik motifs, adapted to the form and texture of the garment. The repeated forms create a continuous rhythm across the shirt, giving the textile the character of a patterned batik rather than a composition organised around a single central motif.

Roy Chowdhury retained the natural sogan brown of the dye, allowing its warm, earthy tone to work in close relation with the natural golden texture of tussar. The restrained colour and repeated Javanese-inspired pattern give the shirt a distinctive balance of materiality, ornament and wearability, bringing a Javanese textile vocabulary into a personal garment made at Santiniketan.

imageAlt: Batik silk sari designed by Jamuna Sen, made by Karu Sangha
attribution: Made by Karu Sangha; individual maker unknown

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik; wax resist and dyes

summary: This silk sari was produced by Karu Sangha, an association of women trained at Kala Bhavana, Santiniketan, during the 1970s–1980s.
description: Although the individual maker of this sari is unknown, it can be associated with Karu Sangha, whose members played an important role in the early commercialisation of Santiniketan batik. The women were trained in the artistic and technical traditions of Kala Bhavana and became particularly known for their ability to reproduce the designs of Jamuna Sen and Gouri Bhanja with remarkable precision.

The sari features a diagonal composition of foliage in acid tones, with elongated leaves and sinuous tendrils that interlace across the surface. The treatment of the foliage recalls the visual language of Ajanta, particularly in the fluid relationship between leaves and tendrils, which merge into an organic, continuous rhythm rather than appearing as isolated botanical forms.

The unnamed maker is significant to the history of the textile. While Jamuna Sen’s design authorship is identified, the skilled woman who translated that design into silk through wax-resist and dyeing remains unrecorded. This distinction reflects the collaborative nature of Santiniketan’s batik production, in which designs developed within Kala Bhavana circulated through the skilled hands of women practitioners whose individual contributions were often absorbed into the collective identity of organisations such as Karu Sangha. The sari thus preserves both a recognisable artistic vocabulary and the traces of an otherwise unnamed maker’s technical expertise.

imageAlt: Batik silk sari by Manjushree Saren

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik; wax resist and dyes

summary: This monochromatic batik sari was made by Manjushree Saren in the 1970s, with the leaf as its central motif.
description: Rather than depicting a single botanical form, the design brings together leaves of different shapes and configurations, placing them against one another to create a rhythmic and varied composition. The subtle differences in contour and proportion allow the repeated forms to generate movement across the length of the sari.

Saren’s close association with nature was rooted in her childhood in Santiniketan. Her father, known as Debi da, was a professor in the Department of Botany at Visva-Bharati, and her early familiarity with the diversity and structure of plant life deeply informed her visual vocabulary. This intimate engagement with nature finds expression in her treatment of the leaf, which is observed, abstracted and reconfigured through the medium of batik.

The monochromatic palette draws attention to the silhouette and structure of each leaf, while their placement against one another creates a continuous rhythm across the textile. The sari reflects a distinctly Santiniketan approach to textile design, in which close observation of the natural world becomes a source for abstraction and pattern.

imageAlt: Batik silk sari by Manjushree Saren

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik; wax resist and dyes

summary: In this batik sari, Manjushree Saren moves beyond the Ajanta-inspired vocabulary evident in some of her earlier work, developing a more freely composed language of lotus and foliage.
description: The lotus is treated in a simplified, graphic manner, while the conjoined leaves and vegetal forms are reconfigured into a more fluid and contemporary pattern. Their interlocking arrangement creates a sense of continuity across the surface of the sari.

The use of acid colours gives the composition a striking visual intensity. Equally important is Saren’s use of dots as fillers: scattered across the ground and between the principal motifs, they are not merely decorative additions but become an integral component of the composition. Their repetition establishes rhythm, fills the spaces between the larger forms and helps bind the different elements into a unified field.

The sari demonstrates Saren’s continuing engagement with nature while showing her willingness to reinterpret botanical forms through the formal possibilities of batik. Here, lotus, foliage, colour and dots work together as elements of an integrated pattern, revealing a distinctively individual approach to Santiniketan textile design.

imageAlt: Batik silk sari designed by Jamuna Sen, made by Karu Sangha
attribution: Made by Karu Sangha; individual maker unknown

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik; wax resist and dyes

summary: This sari was produced by Karu Sangha in the 1980s, from a design by Jamuna Sen.
description: The individual maker remains unnamed, reflecting the collective nature of Karu Sangha’s production, in which the work of skilled women was often identified through the association rather than by individual name.

Set against a brown ground, the sari is covered with a closely knit composition of white alpona-inspired forms. The dense arrangement creates an effect reminiscent of alpona drawn directly onto a surface: rather than appearing as isolated motifs, the white lines and forms come together as a continuous, compact field. The close spacing gives the design a strong visual rhythm while allowing the underlying brown ground to remain an active part of the composition.

The design also demonstrates an economy of colour and production. Restricting the sari to a brown ground and a single contrasting white design means that the textile requires only one dyeing process, making it relatively straightforward and economical to produce. Such considerations were important to the development of Karu Sangha’s commercial batik, where the visual language of Kala Bhavana could be translated into designs that were both distinctive and practical for repeated production.

Here, Jamuna Sen’s compact composition brings together the visual character of hand-drawn alpona with the efficiencies of batik production, illustrating how Santiniketan’s artistic vocabulary was adapted for a growing commercial textile market.

imageAlt: Batik and tie-dye silk handkerchief by Prabir Biswas

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik and tie-dye; wax resist

summary: This handkerchief was made by Prabir Biswas in the 1970s under the guidance of Gouri Bhanja, and may be among the earliest, possibly the first, batik handkerchiefs produced in Santiniketan.
description: Combining wax-resist batik and tie-dye, the small textile demonstrates how techniques associated with Kala Bhavana were adapted to an everyday format.

The design depicts two birds in flight between clouds, creating a light and open composition across the silk. The birds, suspended against the cloud-filled sky, introduce a sense of movement and expansiveness to the otherwise intimate scale of the handkerchief. The interplay of wax-resist lines and tie-dyed passages contributes to the atmospheric quality of the scene.

The handkerchief is significant for its early experimentation with batik beyond the sari and larger textile formats. Its modest scale and everyday function reveal the versatility of the medium, while the combination of batik and tie-dye points to an exploratory approach to resist techniques. Made under Gouri Bhanja’s guidance, it belongs to the formative period of Santiniketan batik, when artists and practitioners were extending the possibilities of the technique into new forms and uses.

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Textile, batik; wax resist and dyes

summary: This batik scroll was made by Bani Biswas at Kala Bhavana in the 1970s, depicting birds in flight across an expansive sky.
description: The birds are distributed across the textile in different positions, creating a sense of movement and spaciousness, while the open ground evokes the changing expanse of the sky.

The work is particularly notable for its sophisticated handling of colour and tonal gradation. Natural and acid dyes are used together, moving from the lightest shades to progressively deeper tones. This gradual build-up of colour creates depth and atmosphere, while the wax-resist process allows the forms to be articulated with the precision of drawing.

In works such as this, batik begins to function less as a technique for decorating a textile and more as a medium for making paintings. The fabric becomes a pictorial surface, and wax and dye take on the roles of line, colour and tonal modulation. The scroll therefore belongs to an important moment in the development of Santiniketan batik, when practitioners at Kala Bhavana were expanding the medium beyond wearable textiles and exploring its possibilities as an independent form of visual expression.

imageAlt: Batik cotton textile by Bani Biswas
summary: This batik textile was made by Bani Biswas at Kala Bhavana in the 1970s, using myrobalan and catechu as natural dyes on cotton.
description: The use of these dyes has resulted in colours that have softened and faded over time, giving the textile a subdued, atmospheric quality.

The composition is deliberately restrained, with a largely empty central field framed by alpona-inspired designs at either end. The contrast between the open centre and the more densely patterned borders creates a sense of balance, while the end motifs provide the textile with a clear visual rhythm.

Its long, narrow format suggests that it may originally have been used as an uttariya, a cloth worn or draped over the upper body. The work is an example of Bani Biswas’s engagement with natural dyes and the possibilities of batik as both a textile technique and a mode of visual composition, in which the unadorned ground is as important to the design as the decorated ends.

imageAlt: Batik silk sari, possibly designed by Nandalal Bose
attribution: Possibly designed by Nandalal Bose or an unnamed artist

facts.label: Materials & techniques
facts.value: Silk, batik; wax resist and dyes

summary: This batik sari, made between the 1930s and 1950s, reflects the influence of Nandalal Bose and the artistic environment of Santiniketan.
description: Its precise designer is unknown: the design may have been created by Nandalal himself or by an unnamed artist working in response to his visual language, particularly the Ajanta-inspired murals and paintings developed at Santiniketan.

At the centre of the composition is a tree with expansive, spreading branches, rendered not simply as a naturalistic botanical form but as a distinctive design in itself. The branching structure extends across the textile with a rhythmic quality, transforming the tree into a pictorial and decorative motif. Its treatment recalls the organic forms and flowing lines associated with Nandalal’s engagement with Indian mural traditions and the visual vocabulary of Ajanta.

The sari borders are organised into discrete segments or blocks, each containing foliage and other decorative forms. Rather than following a single continuous border pattern, these framed sections create a sequence of visual units, giving the edges of the sari a measured rhythm and allowing different motifs to coexist within the larger composition.

The sari is significant as an example of how Nandalal Bose’s artistic vocabulary circulated beyond his own works, entering the realm of textile design through imitation, adaptation and reinterpretation. It demonstrates the ways in which the Ajanta-inspired visual language cultivated at Santiniketan could be translated into batik and adapted to the structure of the sari.

imageAlt: Batik cotton uttariya by Sumitra Narayan
summary: This batik uttariya was made by Sumitra Narayan in the 1980s, using natural dyes.
description: Narayan, who also illustrated the Constitution of India, developed a distinctive approach to batik rooted in the visual traditions of Santiniketan while deliberately moving away from the designs that had become standardised through the commercial production of Karu Sangha.

The textile uses alpona-inspired motifs, arranged across the surface in a fluid and carefully controlled composition. Significantly, the batik is devoid of the characteristic cracks often associated with the technique. Narayan disliked the formation of cracks and deliberately avoided them, allowing the motifs and their outlines to remain clear and uninterrupted. This gives the textile a distinct visual character, in which the precision of the drawn forms takes precedence over the textural effects of crackle.

Her approach demonstrates an individual engagement with batik at a moment when Santiniketan designs were increasingly being reproduced for the commercial market. By returning to the alpona vocabulary while rejecting both the conventions of crackle and the designs institutionalised through Karu Sangha, Narayan developed a more personal language of textile design—one that retained the artistic inheritance of Santiniketan while allowing for greater control over the medium.
